title: Who Is D.B. Cooper? The Hijacker Who Vanished
parts: On the night before Thanksgiving, nineteen seventy one, a man in a suit boarded a plane under a fake name.
He handed a flight attendant a note. It said he had a bomb.
He asked for two hundred thousand dollars, four parachutes, and radio silence.
Then he strapped one on, opened the rear stairs of the plane, and jumped into the night.
He was never seen again. Not his body, not his bones, nothing.
This case is still open, and we will mark every claim: documented, disputed, or no evidence found.
By the end, you will know exactly what the FBI has confirmed about this case, and what is still only a theory.
You will meet three suspects, none of them proven, all of them now dead.
And you will hear about a parachute that resurfaced only months ago, and what the FBI actually said about it.
Welcome to The Everyday Mystery.
First, the hijacking itself.
November twenty fourth, nineteen seventy one. Northwest Orient flight three oh five, a Boeing seven two seven, flying from Portland to Seattle.
A man bought his ticket in cash, under the name Dan Cooper.
Once in the air, he passed that note to a flight attendant, claiming he had a bomb.
He demanded two hundred thousand dollars and four parachutes, ready when the plane landed in Seattle.
The plane landed. He let the passengers go, kept part of the crew, and the money and parachutes came aboard.
Documented, by the FBI's own account.
Then the plane took off again, heading toward Reno, flying low and slow, exactly as he had ordered.
Somewhere over southern Washington, at night, in the rain, he opened the rear stairs and jumped.
He was never seen again.
Even the FBI treats his fate as an open question, not a conclusion. The jump: documented. What happened after it: disputed.
It is still the only unsolved hijacking in American commercial aviation history.
Nine years later, a clue surfaced.
February tenth, nineteen eighty. An eight year old boy found rotting cash buried in a sandbar on the Columbia River.
The serial numbers matched Cooper's ransom. Around five thousand eight hundred dollars, out of the original two hundred thousand.
It is still the only piece of physical evidence ever recovered.
Documented. But it deepens the mystery. It does not solve it.
July eighth, twenty sixteen. The FBI announced it was redirecting its resources.
Not solved. Inactive. They said no tip had ever led to what they called a definitive identification.
They would still look at new physical evidence. Just not new theories. Documented.
Over the decades, three men were named as suspects. None of them confirmed.
Richard McCoy copied the method almost exactly, months later, in a hijacking of his own. But witnesses from the first flight said he didn't match.
Kenneth Christiansen worked for the same airline. His family came forward after his death. His DNA didn't match evidence left on the plane.
Robert Rackstraw, a former paratrooper, was called a "suspect of consensus" by one documentary team. He denied it until he died, in twenty nineteen.
None of the three was ever formally charged. The FBI never confirmed any of them.
Disputed, every one. These are real people, and none of this was ever proven.
And then, in twenty twenty two, a new piece turned up.
A YouTuber found a military style parachute rig in an outbuilding, on property that once belonged to suspect Richard McCoy's family.
McCoy's own children believe it proves their father was Cooper.
In twenty twenty four, the FBI actually seized that parachute, along with other evidence from the property.
They tested it for almost two years.
In December of twenty twenty five, they gave it back. According to McCoy's son, an agent told him the material was, quote, "not being credited or discredited."
Not a yes. Not a no. The FBI either keeps evidence for trial, or returns it. This one came back.
So let's count what we actually know.
The hijacking, the demand, the jump itself: documented.
The money found in nineteen eighty, and the case closing in twenty sixteen: documented.
Every single suspect, and that parachute from twenty twenty five: still no proof, either way.
So, who was D.B. Cooper?
After fifty four years, the honest answer is still: we don't know, and neither does the FBI.
And that leaves one question for next time: if a parachute can sit in an FBI lab for two years and still prove nothing, what would actual proof even look like?
